chapter: Moten band, Kansas City and the evolution of jazz
title: Learning from records and the growth of the band's size
summary: Players learned from records and each other, while critics invented labels. Band size grew from ten pieces; Cab's reed section went from two altos and a tenor to three altos and a tenor with his arrival.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: I guess -- you know, you saying that
you learned from records and all that, Henderson's band and Trumbower and whatever, so once records came in and people were able to buy records --

Right. And then you learn from each other as you went, and those same guys had to learn from listening to records. So everybody learned from each other. And that's the way the whole thing did. But I think the critics and a lot of people that weren't musicians, that write the books and things, they put these cliches on jazz and bebop and all that. It's just the evolution of jazz and the thing just kept on evolving from the way I used to play it by ear until the way -- then I began to learn about chords and harmony and learn how to use these tools to play. And then like they started with -- I said before, many kinds of combinations. Finally they had a set combination for a ten piece band with two trumpets, and a trumpet and two altos and the tenor. Then they finally added on another tenor then they finally added another -- in fact the first -- when I joined Cab Calloway he only had two altos and a tenor and when he added me he had three altos and a tenor, see.

And then eventually the thing became a standard style where they had two altos, two tenors and a baritone. And the trumpet started doing it. But it was an evolution. But everybody was still playing the same thing but it was just getting to be a more involved harmonic thing from playing
